source_text: ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΙΔʹ. Κατὰ μεθυόντων. Κινεῖ μέν με πρὸς τὸν λόγον τὰ ἑσπερινὰ θεά ματα· κατέχει δέ μου πάλιν τὴν ὁρμὴν, καὶ ἀπαμ βλύνει τὴν προθυμίαν τῶν προλαβόντων πόνων τὸ ἄκαρπον. Ἐπεὶ καὶ γεωργὸς, τῶν πρώτων αὐτῷ σπερμάτων μὴ ἐκφυέντων, ὀκνηρότερός ἐστι πρὸς τὸ δεύτερον ταῖς αὐταῖς ἀρούραις πάλιν ἐγκαταβάλλειν. Εἰ γὰρ ἐπὶ τοσαύταις παραινέσεσιν, ἃς ἔν τε τῷ προλαβόντι χρόνῳ παρακαλοῦντες ὑμᾶς οὐ διελίπομεν, καὶ ἐφεξῆς τῶν ἑπτὰ τούτων τῆς νηστείας ἑβδομάδων νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας διαμαρτυρό μενοι ὑμῖν τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τῆς χάριτος τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐκ ἐπαυσάμεθα, οὐδὲν γέγονεν ὄφελος· ἐπὶ ποίαις ἐλπίσι διαλεχθῶμεν σήμερον; Ὢ πόσας νύκτας εἰκῆ ἠγρυπνήσατε! πόσας ἡμέρας εἰκῆ συνηθροίσθητε! εἴ γε καὶ εἰκῆ. Ὁ γὰρ ἐν προκοπῇ γενόμενος ἀγαθῶν ἔργων, εἶτα παλινδρομήσας πρὸς τὴν ἀρχαίαν συν ήθειαν, οὐ μόνον τὸν ἐπὶ τοῖς πεπονημένοις μισθὸν ἐζημιώθη, ἀλλὰ καὶ βαρυτέρας ἀξιοῦται τῆς κατακρίσεως· ὅτι, γευσάμενος καλὸν Θεοῦ ῥῆμα, καὶ γνώσεως μυστηρίων ἀξιωθεὶς, πάντα προέδωκεν, ἡδονῇ βραχείᾳ δελεασθείς. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἐλάχιστος συγγνωστός ἐστιν ἐλέους· δυνατοὶ δὲ, φησὶ, δυνατῶς ἐτασθήσονται. Μία ἑσπέρα, καὶ μία προσβολὴ τοῦ ἐχθροῦ πάντα τὸν πόνον ἐκεῖνον διέλυσε καὶ ἠφάνισε. Ποία οὖν προθυμία τοῦ νῦν λόγου; Ὥστε κἂν ἐσιώπησα, εὖ ἴστε, εἰ μὴ ἐφοβούμην τὸ ὑπόδειγμα τοῦ Ἱερεμίου, ὃς, πρὸς ἀπειθῆ λαὸν φθέγγεσθαι μὴ βουλόμενος, ἔπαθεν ἐκεῖνα ἅπερ αὐτὸς διηγήσατο· ὅτι ἐγένετο αὐτῷ πῦρ ἐν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις, καὶ παρεῖτο πάντοθεν, καὶ οὐκ ἠδύνατο φέρειν. Γυναῖκες ἀκόλαστοι, ἐπιλαθόμεναι τοῦ φόβου τοῦ Θεοῦ, τοῦ πυρὸς τοῦ αἰωνίου καταφρονήσασαι, ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τοιαύτῃ, ὅτε αὐτὰς ἐχρῆν διὰ τὴν ἀνάμνησιν τῆς ἀναστάσεως καθῆσθαι ἐν τοῖς οἵ κοις, καὶ ἔννοιαν λαμβάνειν τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης, καθ' ἣν ἀνοιγήσονται μὲν οἱ οὐρανοὶ, ἐπιφανήσεται δὲ ἡμῖν ὁ κριτὴς ἐξ οὐρανῶν, καὶ σάλπιγγες Θεοῦ, καὶ ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν, καὶ κρίσις δικαία, καὶ ἀντί δοσις ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τὸ ἔργον αὐτοῦ· ἀντὶ τοῦ ταῦτα ἔχειν ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς, καὶ καθαίρειν μὲν ἑαυτῶν τὰς καρδίας ἀπὸ πονηρῶν ἐνθυμήσεων, ἐξ αλείφειν δὲ τοῖς δάκρυσι τὰ προημαρτημένα, ἑτοιμά ζεσθαι δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἀπάντησιν τοῦ Χριστοῦ κατὰ τὴν μεγάλην ἡμέραν τῆς ἐπιφανείας αὐτοῦ, ἀποσεισάμεναι τὸν ζυγὸν τῆς δουλείας τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ῥίψα σαι ἀπὸ τῶν κεφαλῶν τὰ τῆς εὐσχημοσύνης καλύμματα, καταφρονήσασαι τοῦ Θεοῦ, καταφρονήσασαι τῶν ἀγγέλων αὐτοῦ, καταναισχυντήσασαι πάσης ἄῤῥενος ὄψεως, σοβοῦσαι τὰς κόμας, σύρουσαι τοὺς χι τῶνας, καὶ τοῖς ποσὶν ἅμα παίζουσαι, ὀφθαλμῷ ἀσελγεῖ, γέλωτι ἐκκεχυμένῳ πρὸς ὄρχησιν ἐκμανεῖσαι, πᾶσαν νέων ἀκολασίαν ἐφ' ἑαυτὰς προσ καλούμεναι, ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τῆς πόλεως μαρτυ ρίοις χοροὺς συστησάμεναι, ἐργαστήριον τῆς οἰκείας αὐτῶν ἀσχημοσύνης τοὺς ἡγιασμένους τόπους πεποίηνται. Ἐμίαναν μὲν τὸν ἀέρα τοῖς ᾄσμασι τοῖς πορνικοῖς, ἐμίαναν δὲ τὴν γῆν τοῖς ἀκαθάρτοις ποσὶν, ἣν ἐν ταῖς ὀρχήσεσι κατεκρότησαν, θέατρον ἑαυταῖς νεανίσκων ὄχλον περιστησάμεναι, σοβάδες ὄντως καὶ παράφοροι παντελῶς, μανίας οὐδε μίαν ὑπερβολὴν ἀπολείπουσαι. Ταῦτα πῶς μὲν σιωπήσω; πῶς δὲ κατ' ἀξίαν ὀδύρωμαι; Οἶνος ἡμῖν τῶν ψυχῶν τούτων τὴν ζημίαν ἐποίησεν· οἶνος, τὸ παρὰ Θεοῦ δῶρον εἰς παραμυθίαν τῆς ἀσθενείας δεδομένον τοῖς σωφρονοῦσιν· ὅπλον δὲ νῦν γενόμενον ἀκολασίας τοῖς ἀσελγαίνουσιν.
thought_title: One evening undoes the Lenten labor
orientation: Basil opens his homily by lamenting that the shameful sights of the previous evening have undone all his Lenten exhortations to his congregation.
pass_a_gloss: Homily 14. Against drunkards. The evening sights move me toward the word; but again the fruitlessness of the previous labors holds back my impulse and dulls my eagerness. Since also a farmer, when his first seeds do not sprout for him, is more reluctant to cast seed a second time into the same fields. For if upon so many exhortations, which in the previous time we did not cease making to you as we urged you, and in succession during these seven weeks of fasting night and day we did not stop testifying to you the Gospel of the grace of God, no benefit has come about; upon what hopes shall we converse today? O how many nights you kept vigil in vain! how many days you gathered together in vain! if indeed also in vain. For the one who has come into progress of good works, then has run back to the old habit, not only has lost the reward for the things labored over, but also is deemed worthy of heavier condemnation; because, having tasted the good word of God, and having been deemed worthy of knowledge of mysteries, he betrayed everything, lured by brief pleasure. For the least one is pardonable of mercy; but the powerful, it says, will be powerfully tested. One evening, and one assault of the enemy dissolved and obliterated all that labor. What eagerness then for the present word? So that even if I had kept silent, know well, if I did not fear the example of Jeremiah, who, not wishing to speak to a disobedient people, suffered those things which he himself recounted; that fire came to be in his inward parts, and he gave way on every side, and he was not able to bear it. Wanton women, having forgotten the fear of God, having despised the eternal fire, on such a day, when they ought because of the remembrance of the resurrection to sit in their houses, and to take thought of that day, on which the heavens will be opened, and the judge will appear to us from the heavens, and trumpets of God, and resurrection of the dead, and righteous judgment, and recompense to each according to his work; instead of having these things in their thoughts, and cleansing their hearts from evil thoughts, and wiping away with tears the things previously sinned, and preparing for the meeting of Christ according to the great day of his appearing, having shaken off the yoke of the slavery of Christ, having cast from their heads the veils of modesty, having despised God, having despised his angels, having utterly shamed every male gaze, tossing their hair, trailing their tunics, and playing with their feet at the same time, with wanton eye, with poured-out laughter, driven mad to dancing, summoning upon themselves every lust of young men, having formed choruses in the martyrs' shrines before the city, they have made the holy places a workshop of their own shamelessness. They defiled the air with their pornographic songs, and they defiled the earth with their unclean feet, which they stamped in their dances, having surrounded themselves with a crowd of young men as a theater, truly wanton and utterly deranged, leaving no excess of madness. How shall I keep silent about these things? How shall I lament them worthily? Wine made for us the loss of these souls; wine, the gift from God given for the comfort of weakness to the self-controlled; but now having become a weapon of lust for the licentious.

choices.why: The noun with article names the quality of bearing no fruit, matching Basil's agricultural metaphor of seeds that did not sprout.
The compound verb conveys a return to a previous state, matching Basil's image of regression from progress in good works.
The pluperfect passive of παρίημι means he was undone or collapsed, not paralyzed; it conveys yielding on every side under the prophetic burden.
The masculine singular refers to a person of least standing or capacity, not to a sin; the syntax pairs it with δυνατοί (the powerful) in the following clause.
The rare adjective describes women who toss themselves about in a provocative manner, matching the preceding verbs σοβοῦσαι and the context of shameless dancing.
The term denotes a place of production or manufacture, here ironically applied to holy places turned into a site producing shamelessness.

pass_b_english: The sights of this evening move me to speak, but the fruitlessness of my previous labors holds back my impulse and dulls my eagerness. A farmer, when his first seeds do not sprout, is more reluctant to cast seed into the same furrows a second time. If, after all the exhortations we never stopped offering you in the time before, and after these seven weeks of fasting when night and day we did not cease solemnly testifying to you the Gospel of God's grace, nothing has come of it—on what hopes shall I speak today? Oh, how many nights you kept vigil in vain! How many days you gathered in vain! If indeed it was in vain. For the one who has made progress in good works and then has run back to his old habits not only forfeits the reward for his labors but deserves a heavier condemnation, because he tasted the good word of God and was counted worthy of the knowledge of mysteries, yet betrayed everything, lured by a brief pleasure. The one with little is pardonable and receives mercy, but the powerful, it says, will be powerfully tested. One evening, and one assault of the enemy, dissolved and obliterated all that labor. What eagerness, then, can there be for this present word? I would have kept silent, know well, had I not feared the example of Jeremiah, who, when he did not want to speak to a disobedient people, suffered those things he himself described: that fire came into his inward parts, and he gave way on every side, and could not bear it. Wanton women, forgetting the fear of God, despising the eternal fire, on such a day—when they ought to have sat in their homes because of the remembrance of the resurrection and taken thought of that day when the heavens will be opened, and the Judge will appear to us from heaven, and there will be trumpets of God, and resurrection of the dead, and righteous judgment, and recompense to each according to his work—instead of holding these things in their thoughts, and cleansing their hearts from evil imaginations, and wiping away with tears their former sins, and preparing to meet Christ on the great day of his appearing, they shook off the yoke of Christ's service, cast the veils of modesty from their heads, despised God, despised his angels, were shameless before every male gaze, tossing their hair, trailing their tunics, and playing with their feet at the same time, with wanton eye and unrestrained laughter driven mad into dancing, calling upon themselves every lust of young men, forming choruses at the martyrs' shrines before the city, and making the holy places a workshop of their own shamelessness. They defiled the air with their songs of fornication, and defiled the earth with their unclean feet as they stamped it in their dances, surrounding themselves with a crowd of young men as their theater—truly wanton and utterly deranged, leaving no excess of madness undone. How shall I keep silent about these things? How shall I lament them as they deserve? Wine has brought this ruin upon these souls of ours—wine, the gift given by God for the comfort of weakness to the self-controlled, but now become a weapon of lust for the licentious.

problems.why: 'Pornographic' is anachronistic modern sense; 'songs of prostitution/fornication' or 'lewd songs'
'Shamed' reverses agency; they were shameless before/shamed themselves before every male gaze, not shamed the gaze
problems.ruling: καταναισχυντήσασαι = 'acting shamelessly'; 'shamed every male gaze' reverses agency, misleading reader.

fixed: Changed 'pornographic songs' to 'songs of fornication': the source 'ᾄσμασι τοῖς πορνικοῖς' refers to songs of fornication/prostitution, not the modern concept of pornography.

Changed 'shamed every male gaze' to 'were shameless before every male gaze': the source 'καταναισχυντήσασαι πάσης ἄῤῥενος ὄψεως' means they acted shamelessly before every male gaze, not that they shamed the gaze itself.

dismissed.quote: The one with little is pardonable and receives mercy
dismissed.why: ἐλάχιστος means 'the least/slightest' (sin/offense), not 'the one with little'; συγγνωστός means 'excusable', not 'pardonable and receives mercy'
dismissed.note: This is Wisdom 6:6, where ἐλάχιστος is the lowly person, not the 'least offense'; the English sense is acceptable.

dismissed.quote: but the powerful, it says, will be powerfully tested
dismissed.why: δυνατοὶ here means 'the mighty/great ones' (those with much knowledge/responsibility), not 'powerful' in a general sense; ἐτασθήσονται means 'will be examined/judged', not 'tested'
dismissed.note: 'The powerful will be powerfully tested' is the standard rendering of Wisdom 6:6.

dismissed.quote: surrounding themselves with a crowd of young men as their theater
dismissed.why: θέατρον is the object, not 'as their theater'; they made the crowd of young men a theater for themselves (i.e., put themselves on display)
dismissed.note: 'Surrounding themselves with a crowd of young men as their theater' renders the Greek exactly.

dismissed.quote: leaving no excess of madness undone
dismissed.why: ἀπολείπουσαι means 'leaving behind', not 'leaving undone'; they surpass every excess of madness, not fail to complete it
dismissed.note: 'Leaving no excess of madness undone' is the right idiom: they committed every excess, which is what οὐδεμίαν ἀπολείπουσαι means.
